item.title: [9] Capturing α-synuclein polymorphism with AlphaFold 3 and rivals
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Benchmarks AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2 and OpenFold 3 on sampling alpha-synuclein fibril polymorphs and shows template steering recovers 13 of 16 folds, a direct evaluation of cofolding models' multi-state sampling and what they over-represent.

Price, R. M., LaCourse, B., Voorspoels, A., Elliott, L. G. et al.

Amyloid fibrils formed by a single protein can adopt many distinct folds, or polymorphs, which differ between diseases and shape the surfaces available to therapeutics and diagnostics. Whether deep-learning structure prediction can capture this diversity is unclear, and the field lacks an objective definition of a polymorph from which to judge this. Here we cluster the -synuclein structures in the Protein Data Bank by TM-score, giving an objective reference set of known polymorphs. Against this reference we assess AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2 and OpenFold 3 run through ABCFold. All three produced fibril-like assemblies, though they differed in which polymorphs they reached. With templates included as default the methods over-represented the dominant fold. When untemplated the methods produced a substantial number of models matching no known structure, a subset of which have the stacking geometry of genuine fibrils. Supplying a polymorph as a template recovered 13 of 16 target folds, but only when alignment depth and the number of modelled chains were varied together. These results establish that current methods sample real -synuclein structural space and can be steered through it, and provide a framework for assessing prediction methods on amyloid targets.

item.title: [9] ConforFlux: Particle-Guided Trunk Repulsion for Diverse Protein Conformations
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

ConforFlux does inference-time repulsion guidance on Boltz-2 trunk embeddings to sample diverse conformations (also tested on OpenFold3 and Protenix), directly overlapping your embedding-optimization steering for ensembles and a paper you would be surprised to miss.

Suzuki, S., Amagasa, T.

Deep learning models for protein structure prediction achieve near-experimental accuracy on individual folds, yet their default inference samples concentrate around a single dominant conformation. We introduce ConforFlux, an inference-time procedure for Boltz-2 that couples parallel structure-prediction trajectories through a pairwise C-RMSD repulsion gradient on the trunk's single and pair embeddings. The updated trunk conditions every subsequent denoising step without retraining the model. On four conformational-change categories, ConforFlux improves the per-state success rate over default Boltz-2 by 3-17 percentage points, with increased clashscores. The procedure also improves coverage on OpenFold3 and Protenix. On targets whose two reference structures were released after each model's training cutoff, guidance improves coverage of both states on all three models. On the human dopamine transporter, ConforFlux samples inward conformations absent from 500 default samples.

item.title: [8] Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Distills the AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2 diffusion modules from 200 steps to eight and pairs this with physical steering at inference, which directly affects the cost and behavior of the cofolding models you steer in sampleworks.

Vinay Saji Mathew, Soundar Kumara, Gretta Kellogg, William K. M. Lai

arXiv:2610.23703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

item.title: [8] Normalizing Flow Maps
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Normalizing Flow Maps give a new model class combining few-step flow maps with exact likelihoods, with state-of-the-art results on Boltzmann-generator equilibrium sampling for peptides, which bears on equilibrium ensemble emulation and likelihood-based steering.

Francesco M. Ruscio, Timothy James Hitge, Fred Zhangzhi Peng, Danyal Rehman, Zander W. Blasingame, Nicholas M. Boffi, Michael M. Bronstein, Alexander Tong, Avishek Joey Bose

arXiv:2610.22711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable approaches to learning neural dynamical systems have placed diffusion, flow matching, and few-step generators in flow maps at the forefront of generative modeling. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps (NFM), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFMs learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction. To enable scalable training of NFMs, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFMs that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks $\ell_2$-based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process. On conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, NFMs achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFMs outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.

item.title: [8] Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Distance-AF Multimer steers AlphaFold-Multimer predictions with user-supplied experimental distance restraints on complexes, closely paralleling your data-guided structure-model steering work and extending a method you likely know.

Ling, K., Zhang, Y., Zhang, Z., Nakamura, T. et al.

The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains.

item.title: [7] Learning the Shared Latent Structure of Cryo-EM Inverse Problems
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

EMber is a cryo-EM foundation model pretrained on 50M particle images and 214 EMPIAR datasets that discriminates conformations and estimates conformational populations, relevant to cryo-EM heterogeneity, though it is a representation model rather than a generative prior.

Nithin Chalapathi, Theo Sternlieb, Ethan Han, Sonya M. Hanson, Pilar Cossio, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, Ritwik Gupta

arXiv:2610.22523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding biomolecular function requires characterizing three-dimensional structure and conformational variability, for which cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a powerful tool. Cryo-EM produces noisy two-dimensional particle images in which molecular structure, particle pose, and imaging conditions are jointly encoded. Recovering biological information from these observations spans inverse problems including pose estimation, heterogeneity analysis, and reconstruction. These tasks are usually addressed independently despite shared protein structure and image formation, motivating a common representation across inverse problems. Since biologically meaningful differences may be spatially localized, we study self-distillation with complementary global and masked patch objectives. Because experimental dataset discrimination can reflect acquisition-specific cues, we develop controlled synthetic and experimental evaluations and find that structural discrimination benefits from dense spatial features. We introduce the EMber family of vision transformers, pre-trained on >50 million experimental particle images from 214 EMPIAR datasets together with simulated projections from 268,000 molecular assemblies. EMber improves upon existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by 14.85 and 14.26 percentage points, estimates conformational populations to within 1.59pp error with a linear probe, and produces particle assignments yielding reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs. We demonstrate how to learn representations that capture biological information for use across multiple cryo-EM inverse problems.

item.title: [7] Generative steering to adapt proteins beyond native biological contexts
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

ProVADA is a test-time steering framework with an annealed population sampler for a pretrained protein generator, with wet-lab validation, but it targets sequence-level property design rather than structural ensembles or experimental-data restraints.

Zhang, X., Lu, W. S., Viggiano, B., Reynolds, K. et al.

Proteins evolved for native biological contexts often fail when deployed in new cellular environments or therapeutic settings. We present ProVADA, a test-time framework that steers a pretrained protein generator toward externally defined properties while preserving functional constraints. Its Mixture-Adaptation Directed Annealing sampler combines coordinated mutations, population selection, and annealing to navigate rugged objective landscapes. Experimentally, ProVADA converted secreted human renin into an active, drug-inhibitable cytosolic protease and extensively deimmunized two murine single-chain antibody fragments to reduce HLA visibility while retaining antigen recognition. ESCAPE-seq measurements confirmed substantial depletion of HLA-I binder peptides across alleles. Deimmunized FMC63 variants retained CAR-T-cell killing and showed fewer binders than a tested humanized comparator. Together, these results demonstrate that broad sequence redesign can adapt functional proteins to non-native biological contexts.

item.title: [10] RGI-Toolkit: Differentiable Restraints for Controllable Biomolecular Structure Prediction
item.description:
Score 10/10 · bioRxiv

RGI-Toolkit packages differentiable restraint-guided inference across six structure predictors including AlphaFold3, which is nearly exactly the modular steering-with-restraints platform you are building in sampleworks and you will want to compare against it.

Hori, T., Moriwaki, Y., Ishitani, R.

Diffusion-based models have substantially advanced biomolecular structure prediction. Within this framework, restraint-guided inference (RGI) corrects the denoiser output at each reverse-diffusion step using a differentiable restraint loss, allowing available experimental information, stereochemical requirements, or a specified target conformational state to be incorporated into predictions without retraining the model. Here, we present RGI-Toolkit, a general-purpose Python library that makes RGI available for a range of structure predictors. The toolkit consolidates restraint definition, atom selection, loss evaluation, and coordinate optimization into a shared, backend-agnostic engine, limiting predictor-specific code to a thin preprocessing adapter and a single hook in the denoising loop. Restraints on distances, angles, and dihedrals, on deviations from reference structures, and on user-defined reaction coordinates, together with ligand conformer restraints, are all specified in a common configuration format. The toolkit currently supports six predictors, including AlphaFold3. Across all six predictors, conformer restraints eliminated chirality and cis/trans errors in the predicted ligands and improved their local geometry, while geometric and custom restraints systematically shifted the sampled protein conformations toward the specified target states. RGI-Toolkit thus provides a unified framework for integrating experimental information and prior geometric knowledge into structure prediction and for generating biomolecular structures with specified conformational and stereochemical properties.

item.title: [9] Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Baker lab trains RF3 to accept atom-pair distance conditions with classifier-free guidance faded over design cycles, plus training-free motif guidance during diffusion sampling, directly relevant to guiding cofolding models with constraints.

Qian, T., Wang, W., Gao, S., Muraishi, A. et al.

De novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7[A] crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.

item.title: [8] Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Noise Policy Optimization learns a flow over the initial noise space to produce reward-tilted outputs from a frozen few-step generator, including protein structure generation, which is a new black-box reward steering idea that is directly relevant to reward guidance of structure models.

Woocheol Shin, Taeyoung Yun, Jiwon Sung, Hyeongyu Kang, Jeongmin Park, Jaewoo Lee, Kyuil Sim, Dohyun Kim, Yutong He, Jinkyoo Park

arXiv:2610.21125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

item.title: [7] Boltzmann generators for amorphous particle systems
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Equivariant Riemannian stochastic-interpolant Boltzmann generators that expose a concrete failure of continuous-flow likelihood reweighting speak directly to the question of whether generative samplers can give exact equilibrium ensembles.

Louis Grenioux, Leonardo Galliano, Ludovic Berthier, Giulio Biroli, Marylou Gabri\'e

arXiv:2512.16607v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling configurations in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators address this problem by employing generative models to propose independent configurations, which are then reweighted via importance sampling using exact likelihood evaluations. Recent Boltzmann Generators based on continuous normalizing flows and flow matching have achieved significant success for particle systems and biomolecules. However, these approaches have not been extended to amorphous materials (glasses), for which equilibrium sampling is notoriously slow. Because of their disordered structure, the invariances and geometrical constraints of amorphous materials differ from those of crystals and biomolecules, preventing the direct use of existing generative models. Here, we develop Boltzmann Generators tailored to amorphous materials by building the required equivariances directly into Riemannian stochastic interpolants. Our framework incorporates periodic boundary conditions and particle symmetries using equivariant graph neural networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate that enforcing physical symmetries significantly improves the accuracy of Boltzmann Generators, but also reveal an intrinsic limitation of the continuous-flow formulation: accumulated numerical errors during likelihood integration break time-reversibility, compromising exact thermodynamic reweighting. These results reveal a fundamental challenge for continuous-flow generative models in statistical mechanics and call for alternative approaches that preserve exact thermodynamic consistency.

item.title: [7] A perturbation theory for Feynman-Kac models and their particle interpretations
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Del Moral and Gerber give time-uniform error bounds for Feynman-Kac models and particle methods, the theoretical foundation of the SMC steering used for diffusion guidance, from the field's leading authority.

Pierre Del Moral, Mathieu Gerber

arXiv:2610.21587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a perturbation analysis of Feynman--Kac models, describing how local errors introduced at each step of the Feynman--Kac recursion propagate over time. Under general conditions on the potential functions and the Markov transitions, which are shown to hold for a large class of state-space models, we prove that the global error for any time horizon $T\geq 1$ is bounded by $C\,\Delta_T\log(1+\Delta_T^{-1})$, where $\Delta_T$ is the largest local error; this bound holds both for the prediction and the updated models. These conditions require no Lyapunov function and no stability of the Markov transitions, and allow for non-compact state spaces: confinement is provided by the potential functions. Our perturbation bounds hold in total variation and in the Kolmogorov norm; for the latter, we extend the Hardy--Krause variation and the Koksma--Hlawka inequality to unbounded domains. Our perturbation theory is applied to derive time-uniform bounds for linearized Kalman filters, Euler schemes for partially observed diffusions and nudged state-space models, as well as high-probability error bounds, uniform over whole trajectories, for particle filters and, more generally, for mean field particle methods such as sequential Monte Carlo and diffusion Monte Carlo algorithms.

item.title: [8] ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

It tests whether coding agents can rebuild ProteinMPNN and RFdiffusion3 from limited descriptions, including a memorisation check, which sits at the intersection of agents for science, protein design tools and the memorise-versus-learn question.

Shiv Muthupandiyan, Tolga H. Dur, Mac Walker, Timo Flesch, Mahmoud Ghanem, Steph Suddell, Giles Harper-Donnelly, Sophie Rose, Jasper G\"otting, Coleman Breen, Jake Pencharz

arXiv:2610.19810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

item.title: [7] Steering Diffusion Models to Rare Events with Sequential Monte Carlo
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

DireSMC guides diffusion surrogates via SMC to rare events with calibrated probability estimates, including molecular dynamics emulators, which is relevant to sampling low-population states; it is mostly a known SMC framework applied to a new task, so it is capped here.

Aavash Subedi, Tim Reichelt, Christopher Williams, Philip Stier, Yee Whye Teh, Saifuddin Syed

arXiv:2610.08652v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive simulators in weather prediction, molecular dynamics, and materials design. In these models, computing the probability $p_0[E]$ of an event $E$ is difficult, especially when the event of interest is rare. A stable estimate using Monte Carlo becomes computationally intractable, requiring a growing sample size $\propto\!1/p_0[E]$ to compensate for an increasing rarity. In this paper, we present Diffusion rare event sampling with Sequential Monte Carlo (DireSMC), a sequential Monte Carlo scheme that guides a population of weighted samples towards the rare event, giving access not only to samples but also to a calibrated estimate of its probability. We set up our guidance using an analytical relaxation of the event set, allowing the method to easily extend to a wide range of user-defined rare events. We validate our method on a toy problem with analytical solutions and on a score-based climate emulator, where we obtain accurate rare-event probabilities on a range of rarities from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-5}$, achieving net speed-ups of $9\times$ to $1413\times$ over Monte Carlo.

item.title: [7] Mixed Poisson diffusion models and application to posterior sampling
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Mixed Poisson diffusion models with posterior sampling for Poisson inverse problems are a new diffusion-prior framework for count-based measurements, which is relevant to inverse problems with non-Gaussian noise such as low-dose cryo-EM or X-ray detectors, though no structural application is shown.

Thibaut Pellerin, Alain Durmus, Elinor Berger, Eric Barat

arXiv:2610.20218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models are a powerful framework for learning complex probability distributions. While widely used diffusion models for continuous data rely on Gaussian noising processes, we instead develop diffusion models based on Poisson noise. More precisely, we introduce and study a new mathematical framework, called Mixed Poisson Diffusion Models (MPDM), with noising dynamics driven by multivariate counting processes. Our methodology is motivated by Poisson inverse problems. The success of Gaussian diffusion models has led to their use as prior models in a growing number of posterior sampling methods for inverse problems. However, most of these approaches focus on Gaussian inverse problems, in which observations are generated through a deterministic forward operator corrupted by additive Gaussian noise. By contrast, Poisson inverse problems, where observations are discrete and Poisson distributed, remain comparatively underexplored in this literature. Building on our Poisson generative dynamics, we develop a natural framework for posterior sampling in Poisson inverse problems and derive several posterior sampling algorithms based on the proposed model. We evaluate our approach on realistic Poisson inverse problems and show that the resulting framework is well suited to this class of problems.

item.title: [7] Weighted Adjoint Matching: Finetuning Flow Matching Models with Time-Dependent Control Cost
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Weighted Adjoint Matching adds a time-dependent control cost to reward finetuning of flow and diffusion models, proving equivalence to time-varying KL regularization and improving the reward-versus-diversity tradeoff, which is directly relevant to reward-guided steering that must preserve ensemble diversity.

Eliot Beyler, Francis Bach

arXiv:2610.20035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback--Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.

item.title: [9] Quantifying RNA Folding Equilibria from Unclassified Cryo-EM Particle Images
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Bayesian ensemble reweighting of unclassified cryo-EM particle images to quantify RNA conformational equilibria is a direct experiment-informed ensemble method from the Cossio group, and it is highly relevant to your use of experimental data to constrain ensembles.

Maji, D., Dingeldein, L., Li, M., Astore, M. A. et al.

Functional RNA structures are typically far more dynamic than most proteins solved by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Flexible junctions and weak tertiary contacts produce broad conformational ensembles, and cryo-EM particle classification analyses discard unaligned particles, which inherently contain the information needed to quantify such broad ensembles. Here, we infer compositional and conformational distributions from unclassified particle images by Bayesian ensemble reweighting. We tested our approach on the P4-P6 domain of the Tetrahymena thermophila group I intron, a classic model system of Mg2+-dependent RNA folding. While stable monomeric and dimeric states yielded high-resolution reconstructions, analyses of abundant, flexible conformations required Bayesian ensemble inference. Our approach quantitatively captured the Mg2+-dependent folding transition, indicating that cryo-EM can report the abundance of coexisting RNA states in agreement with bulk solution measurements. These results showcase how quantitative studies of RNA folding can be achieved by combining cryo-EM measurements with statistical ensemble-inference tools.

item.title: [8] zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

zPocket trains pocket-prediction heads on frozen cofolding trunk features and introduces PocketWatch, a benchmark of unseen and cryptic pockets, directly addressing what Boltz-style cofolding representations encode and how to evaluate generalization beyond their training distribution.

Tally Portnoi, Allison M Keys, Benjamin R DiFrancesco, Nate Gruver

arXiv:2610.17696v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.

item.title: [8] A Stochastic Analysis Perspective on Diffusion Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A stochastic-analysis exposition of score-based diffusion models that covers Langevin sampling, denoising score matching, and path-space time reversal is the kind of expository treatment underpinning guidance and posterior sampling that you would want to read.

Stanislas Strasman (SU, LPSM)

arXiv:2610.14133v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative modelling involves two complementary tasks: learning a probabilistic approximation of an unknown data distribution from observations, and designing a tractable mechanism for sampling from this approximation. We present a stochastic-analysis perspective on score-based generative models, connecting ideas from classical sampling theory, score estimation, and diffusion time reversal. We first explain how score functions link Langevin sampling with score matching, and how Gaussian smoothing leads to denoising score matching and multiscale sampling methods. We then emphasize the distinction between dynamics preserving a fixed distribution and dynamics transporting a prescribed family of marginals. This motivates a path-space treatment of diffusion time reversal. Finally, we connect the ideal reverse diffusion with practical generative algorithms.

item.title: [7] Computational design of metalloproteases
item.description:
Score 7/10 · Nature

Baker lab using RFdiffusion to design zinc metalloproteases with a programmable substrate pocket is a major result for the RFdiffusion lineage, though it is mainly a design paper rather than a guidance-method advance.

Anqi Chen, Kejia Wu, Hojae Choi, Preetham Venkatesh et al.

RFdiffusion methods are used to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket, yielding highly active, programmable proteases with potential applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

item.title: [7] ConicFlow: constrained Inference-time optimal control for flow matching models
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

ConicFlow poses constrained inference-time steering of flow-matching models as receding-horizon optimal control with hard terminal constraints and guarantees, a new formulation that could carry over to restraint-satisfying structure sampling.

Shervin Khalafi, Kasra Fallah, Sung Cho, Dongsheng Ding, James Anderson, Alejandro Ribeiro

arXiv:2610.14307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose ConicFlow, which frames constrained sampling from a flow matching model at inference time as an optimal control problem that balances deviation from the pretrained trajectory against reward, subject to hard terminal constraints. We discretize this problem and adapt receding-horizon control, optimizing only a short window of the trajectory at each step for computational tractability. We address the resulting sequence of receding-horizon subproblems with a receding-horizon primal-dual algorithm. Its dual multipliers capture the difficulty of satisfying each constraint and are refined throughout sampling, steering generation toward feasible final samples. We further propose a terminal-estimate variant that avoids accumulating local truncation errors by evaluating the reward and constraints at the predicted terminal point rather than at the end of the current horizon. Under standard regularity assumptions, we establish finite-horizon guarantees on suboptimality. Under convex-affine structure, we derive a sharper bound that scales linearly with omitted horizon length, and we show that the terminal-estimate variant is provably tighter when the flow dynamics change slowly. Experiments in both low- and high-dimensional settings with a recent large-scale flow matching model show that ConicFlow achieves high reward and strong constraint satisfaction while deviating less from the pretrained flow than recent baselines.

item.title: [7] Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Single-protein 3D imaging of erythrocruorin with an XFEL, with the gas-phase heterogeneity limiting resolution, is a striking milestone in single-particle structure determination that you would want to have seen.

Paul Lourdu Xavier, Andrew J. Morgan, Johan Bielecki, Amit K. Samanta, Simon Dold, Chufeng Li, Xinyue Gao, Spencer K. Passmore, Ruslan P. Kurta, Tim B. Berberich, Emiliano De Santis, Wenhui Zhang, Juncheng E, Faisal H. M. Koua, Romain Letrun, Luca Gelisio, Oleksii Turkot, Egor Sobolev, Lukas V. Haas, Jannik L\"ubke, Jingxuan He, Madeline B. F. Memovich, Kevin Janson, Stefanie Lenzen, Safi Rafie-Zinedine, Mansi Butola, Oleksandr Yefanov, Fabian Trost, Chan Kim, Tomas Popelar, Tokushi Sato, Yevheniy Ovcharenko, Rebecca Boll, Sergey Usenko, Thomas M. Baumann, Alberto De Fanis, Bj\"orn Senftleben, Matteo Porro, Andrea Castoldi, Ibrahym Dourki, Cyril Danilevski, Ekaterina Round, Christina Schmidt, Huijong Han, Roberto Alvarez, Ervin Chia, Cornelia Cazey, Carolin Seuring, Ruojie Sha, Maia Azubel, David A. Bushnell, S\'ebastien Boutet, Sergey Ovchinnikov, Adrian P. Mancuso, Michael Meyer, Richard Bean, Anton Barty, Filipe R. N. C. Maia, Richard A. Kirian, Thomas D. Grant, N. Duane Loh, Carl Caleman, Erik G. Marklund, Nadia Zatsepin, Andrew V. Martin, Sa\v{s}a Bajt, Roger D. Kornberg, Jochen K\"upper, Henry N. Chapman

arXiv:2610.11892v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The extremely intense pulses of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) have enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to deliver biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work-flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Based on decades of improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to approximately 20 Angstrom, while the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.

item.title: [7] BridgeTwist: Twisting Schr\"odinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

BridgeTwist brings twisted sequential Monte Carlo to pretrained Schrödinger-bridge models for training-free posterior sampling with a likelihood, which is the same prior-plus-measurement setup as your steering platform though on a new model class and image tasks.

Mengyu Li, Qianqian Qu, Jun S. Liu

arXiv:2610.18658v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schr\"odinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

item.title: [7] Imperfect Verifiers, Exact Targets: Inference-Time Scaling for Continuous Generation
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

CS-VGB recovers the exact reward-tilted target despite imperfect intermediate verifiers via denoise-renoise backtracking, directly addressing the weak spot of noisy guidance signals in inference-time steering.

Kijung Jeon, Molei Tao

arXiv:2610.15281v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling uses additional computation to score intermediate states and steer generation toward better outputs. However, imperfect intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not ensure recovery of the desired reward-tilted distribution. We introduce Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (CS-VGB), an inference-time scaling method for sampling from reward-tilted distributions with continuous generative models through repeated denoising and renoising. With correctly paired denoising and renoising transitions, the stationary distribution of CS-VGB at the clean checkpoint equals the desired reward-tilted target, even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate. Under stated regularity conditions, CS-VGB converges exponentially to the target despite verifier error, and the expected number of updates needed to reach a clean sample grows only linearly with the number of checkpoints. In analytically tractable settings, we empirically demonstrate that CS-VGB recovers the desired reward-tilted distribution despite verifier error, whereas the compared verifier-based sampling methods fail to recover the target under the same verifier errors. We also instantiate the framework with diffusion models and one-step stochastic posterior maps. Across prompt-guided ImageNet generation, facial-attribute generation on CelebA, and multi-robot planning, recurrent CS-VGB search improves reward and task success as inference budgets grow, with image-generation rewards continuing beyond the observed plateaus of denoising-only baselines.

item.title: [7] Calibrating AlphaFold confidence scores for interface quality
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Post-hoc calibration of AlphaFold confidence scores into probabilities of passing a DockQ threshold bears directly on evaluating cofolding models and on reward or ranking signals for steering, though it is a modest methodological contribution.

Sagyndyk Sagadinov, Vsevolod Viliuga, Arne Elofsson

arXiv:2610.17108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used to rank protein complex predictions and to select subsets of models for downstream applications. Although these scores provide strong discriminatory power for distinguishing prediction quality, their numerical values were never intended to represent the probability that a prediction satisfies a given structural quality criterion. In this work, we calibrate commonly used confidence scores to estimate the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen threshold of DockQ, an established measure of interface quality. On antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets, post-hoc isotonic calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving the underlying score ordering. The calibrated probabilities also provide more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a given structural quality threshold. Although the mapping is fitted within a given prediction distribution and therefore transfers imperfectly across prediction domains, we show that reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples. Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and requires no underlying AlphaFold model fine-tuning, it provides a straightforward and customizable way to convert existing model quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.

item.title: [9] AlphaFold3 and Intrinsically Disordered Proteins: Reliable Monomer Prediction, Unpredictable Multimer Performance
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

A systematic AF3 evaluation on disordered proteins showing deterministic, seed-invariant failures in multimers and concluding that ensemble sampling is needed speaks directly to your interest in what cofolding models learn versus memorize and why they fail to sample multiple states.

Dao, T. M., Ghent, S., Uversky, V. N., Rahman, T.

AlphaFold3 represents a major advance in protein structure prediction, yet its performance on intrinsically disordered proteins remains uncharacterized. We present the first systematic evaluation of AF3 on disordered systems, revealing a striking dichotomy. For monomers, AF3's pLDDT scores reliably predict disorder (MCC: 0.693), matching AlphaFold2 and rivaling dedicated predictors. This consistency across fundamentally different architectures confirms that disorder prediction emerges from training data, not model design. For multimers, the picture grows complex. Despite comparable aggregate performance (mean DockQ: 0.563 vs 0.571), AF3 and AF2 achieve these results through fundamentally different mechanisms. Conventional structural features explain 58% of AF2's variance but only 42% of AF3's. Users cannot predict when AF3 will succeed or fail from interface properties alone. On disorder-to-order transitions (MFIB benchmark), both models perform equally well, successfully predicting final folded states. Yet seed variance analysis reveals AF3's failures are deterministic: the model converges to identical structures across independent runs, whether correct or incorrect, indicating rigid structural priors override available information. Our findings establish AF3 as reliable for the prediction of monomer disorder but unpredictable for multimers. Architectural innovation alone cannot overcome training data bias. Progress demands disorder-enriched datasets and ensemble sampling, not merely novel architectures.

item.title: [7] Pre-catalytic activation pathway of the Smc5/6 complex
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Cryo-EM heterogeneity analysis resolving Smc5/6 as a conformational ensemble with a continuous Cross-to-Juxtaposed transition, plus network modeling of the pathway, is a good real-data example of the kind of ensembles your steering work aims to reproduce.

Wong, J. S. K., Loke, M. S., Pradhan, B., Kanno, T. et al.

The Smc5/6 complex (Smc5/6) preserves genome stability through ATP-dependent DNA organization, but the structural details that prime the complex for productive DNA engagement remain unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy and conformational heterogeneity analysis to define the pre-catalytic activation pathway of Smc5/6. We show that in the absence of ATP and DNA, Smc5/6 exists as a heterogeneous conformational ensemble composed predominantly of two conformations termed Bridge and Cross. In the presence of DNA alone, Smc5/6 adopts a Juxtaposed conformation that brings the ATPase heads into proximity, aligning them for nucleotide engagement. With both ATP and DNA associated, Smc5/6 establishes an Engaged architecture, within which DNA stabilizes its head-associated binding cavity through local remodeling of the complex. Conformational heterogeneity analyses suggest a continuous structural transition between the Cross and Juxtaposed states, while anisotropic network modeling identifies the Bridge-Cross-Juxtaposed-Engaged sequence as the mechanically favored pathway connecting the four experimentally observed conformations. Together, these findings support a pre-catalytic conformational pathway for Smc5/6 activation and provide a structural framework for understanding how conformational heterogeneity gives rise to an activation-competent motor state.

item.title: [8] Inference-Time Steering Across Scaffolds and Epitopes for Sample-Efficient De Novo Nanobody Design
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Feynman-Kac and SMC inference-time steering for de novo nanobody design, with dynamic compute allocation across conditioning configurations, is a close cousin of the inference-time steering you build and transfers to allocating budget across conditions.

Mason Minot, Simon Friedensohn, C\'edric R. Weber

arXiv:2610.13844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative molecular design typically relies on over-generation and post-hoc filtering. Inference-time steering methods like Feynman-Kac (FK) steering improve efficiency by biasing trajectories toward high-reward candidates, yet they optimize within a single fixed configuration. In de novo nanobody design, upfront commitment to conditioning choices like scaffold identity or target epitope creates a bottleneck. Since yield varies across these conditions, steering unpromising setups wastes compute. We recast generative condition selection as an inference-time resource-allocation problem. We propose two dynamic budget allocators: a joint Global Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) formulation that steers and allocates compute across configurations concurrently, and a decoupled approach adapting Batched Successive Elimination (BaSE). Empirically, these dynamic allocators increase the yield of designable candidates per GPU-hour nearly 5$\times$ without sacrificing diversity across distinct therapeutic targets and generative configurations.

item.title: [8] Spanning Diffusion and Flow-based Posterior Sampling via Exact Gaussian Conditioning
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

β-Flow unifies flow, diffusion and decorrelated priors for inverse problems through an exact Kalman-style Gaussian conditioning step that needs no network gradients and clarifies the implicit assumptions of existing guided samplers, which bears directly on steering with experimental observations.

Teo Deveney, Lea Bogensperger, Hok Shing Wong

arXiv:2610.13812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-matching and diffusion models are increasingly used as priors for linear inverse problems, however, most methods are bespoke to one class of trajectory prior. Plug-and-play methods have been proposed, however these implicitly decorrelate the guided trajectory, resulting in broad priors that can struggle when data is sparse. This work proposes $\beta$-Flow: a general plug-and-play method indexed by a correlation parameter $\beta$ that generalises over flow, diffusion, and decorrelated priors, and a confidence parameter $\kappa$ that controls how strongly the path distribution is enforced. Each step requires only one forward evaluation of a denoising network, followed by a Gaussian conditioning step. This step is an exact Kalman update that is not dependent on network gradients. We show that many existing guided samplers can be interpreted as instances or approximations of our method, each implicitly using a different trajectory prior and operator in place of the Kalman gain. From this viewpoint, we provide a qualitative comparison of methods in terms of their implicit biases and assumptions. We demonstrate consistently state-of-the-art level performance across 7 inverse problems over 4 datasets in terms of PSNR and SSIM. Moreover, we demonstrate the utility of this prior control, by showing that confident high correlations (strict priors) work best when observations are less informative, while low correlation is preferred when observations are more informative, reflecting the complementary roles of the prior and likelihood in Bayesian inference.

item.title: [8] The CAHRA Challenge: A Community-Wide Assessment of Cryo-EM Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Zhong-lab-led community benchmark with ground-truth datasets for cryo-EM compositional and continuous heterogeneity, giving you an evaluation standard for the heterogeneity methods your ensemble work is measured against.

Feathers, J. R., Heeter, R., Woollard, G., Hanson, S. M. et al.

The ability of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to interrogate the atomic structure and motion of biomolecules has motivated the development of a wide range of algorithms for heterogeneity analysis. However, evaluating and comparing these methods remains challenging because ground-truth structures are generally unknown for experimental samples. Here, we introduce the 2026 Community-Wide Assessment of Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms (CAHRA), a community-wide challenge centered on three benchmark datasets that probe distinct tasks in heterogeneity analysis. These include (1) compositional heterogeneity arising from mixtures of distinct protein complexes, (2) continuous conformational variability and atomic modeling, and (3) entanglement between molecular conformation and particle pose. We describe the design, construction, and validation of these datasets, as well as their use in the recently completed CAHRA Challenge.

item.title: [7] Looking Under the Streetlight: Evaluation in Generative Molecular Dynamics
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A position paper by Olsson, Noé, Rotskoff and Lindorff-Larsen arguing that generative MD evaluation lets models match reported proxies while being wrong on the claimed ensemble properties, directly relevant to how you validate BioEmu-style ensemble emulators.

Simon Olsson, Frank No\'e, Grant M. Rotskoff, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen

arXiv:2610.12518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This position paper argues that the generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) community is not properly evaluating its progress: current evaluations let a model match what is reported while being arbitrarily wrong on what was claimed, which risks over-claiming advantage over classical baselines. This reflects a structural misalignment between common evaluation practices and the scientific tasks the field sets for itself. The reason is that the ground truth---exhaustive molecular dynamics on the systems of interest---is computationally costly, and this cost is what motivates the field. With ground truth inaccessible, evaluation drifts toward convenient proxies, and the resulting norms entrench easily. We identify misaligned evaluation patterns that persist as a community-level equilibrium, and propose concrete observables, reporting standards, and benchmark designs, both computational and experimental, that better reflect what GenMD aspires to deliver. Our aim is to give the field shared language and tools for evaluation that match its scientific ambitions before today's conventions calcify into norms.

item.title: [7] Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

An information-theoretic account of when classifier-free guidance matters during sampling, with a training-free adaptive activation rule that could directly inform guidance schedules in your steering platform.

Jiayang Gao, Tianyi Zheng, Jiayang Zou, Fengxiang Yang, Luyao Fan, Lv Tang, Bo Li, Jia Wang

arXiv:2610.13369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.

item.title: [7] Some remarks on the connection between generative diffusion and optimal transport
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Biroli and Mézard tie diffusion and flow-matching generation to entropic optimal transport and the speciation transition, a theory exposition that sharpens intuition for how diffusion samplers behave.

Giulio Biroli, Marc M\'ezard

arXiv:2610.13614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We discuss three simple connections between generative diffusion and optimal transport. First, the joint law of the data and of their Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noising is, at every time, the solution of an entropic optimal-transport problem, at a temperature set by the noise level. Backward diffusion can consequently be read as an annealing which gradually decreases the entropic regularization. Second, we study the speciation transition--how the modes of the data distribution emerge during generation--and compare how it happens in diffusion and flow matching with respect to optimal transport. Using Gaussian mixtures as high-dimensional example, we show that the dynamical instability through which diffusion and flow matching separate the modes becomes, for optimal transport, an exponentially thin boundary layer at the beginning of generation, which is rounded by entropic regularization. Third, considering a generic forward dynamics with a general confining potential, we show that the backward process driven by the score also satisfies a drift-based variational principle whose minimal cost is the entropy difference between initial and final distributions.

item.title: [7] Sequence context decodes multi-state conformational heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Recovering residue-wise multi-state heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors with a sequence-aware model speaks directly to extracting ensemble information from crystallographic data and could serve as a prior for your refinement work.

Wang, Y., Cai, M., Ma, Y., Shi, T. et al.

Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, yet the overwhelming majority of experimentally determined structures capture only static snapshots, leaving the multi-state heterogeneity that underlies biological activity largely inaccessible. X-ray crystallography, the dominant source of these structures, does carry one experimental proxy for motion, the atomic B-factor, but crystal packing and refinement artifacts frequently obscure its link to solution-state dynamics. Here we show that sequence context is sufficient to decode a protein's multi-state conformational heterogeneity from this seemingly noisy signal. We introduce the B-Factor Corrector (BFC), a fine-tuned protein language model that reframes B-factor analysis from a purely physical calculation into a sequence-context-aware translation task. By leveraging deep contextual embeddings to decouple intrinsic conformational heterogeneity from lattice constraints, BFC recovers the residue-wise heterogeneity ranking derived from crystallographic structural ensembles, reproducing the normalized profile at a Pearson correlation of 0.83 while correcting the distortions that analytical formulas leave in the raw signal. We further demonstrate the utility of this sequence-inferred signal across structural-biology applications: it provides an integrable prior for molecular docking that is statistically equivalent to experimental B-factors, unmasks cryptic conformational heterogeneity essential for chaperone function, and guides the energetic refinement of antibody interfaces to resolve steric conflicts. These results suggest that the static structures of the Protein Data Bank can be effectively repurposed to decode the conformational heterogeneity latent within them.

item.title: [7] Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Claude Code agents autonomously mining 1.9 billion protein clusters and surfacing a new reverse transcriptase family is a concrete, serious example of agents doing computational biology discovery, plus the striking tandem-repeat RT biology.

Yoon, P. H., Athukoralage, J. S., Ameisen, E., Kauderer-Abrams, E. et al.

Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

item.title: [7] Ab initio CryoEM maps minimizing preferred orientation problems in heterogeneous mixtures: ReconSIREN
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

ReconSIREN is an ab initio neural cryo-EM reconstruction method that handles preferred orientation and outputs a conformational landscape, which is directly relevant to heterogeneity modeling, though it is a method variant rather than a conceptual advance.

Herreros, D., Sorzano, C. O. S., Carazo, J. M.

Cryo-Electron Microscopy (CryoEM) Single Particle Analysis (SPA) is pivotal for elucidating protein structures and their conformational dynamics. Several critical steps are required to obtain accurate maps. First, the \textit{ab initio} relative orientations and shifts between images must be determined. Second, the common issue of specimens presenting a preferred orientation should be adequately addressed. Third, all of the above must account for particle flexibility and sample heterogeneity. Additionally, these steps are interrelated, making the search for all these parameters a real challenge when considering convergence robustness. In this context, we present ReconSIREN, a novel deep learning framework that addresses the key steps outlined before in an \textit{ab initio} manner while greatly minimizing one of the most important practical burdens in SPA, namely the errors introduced in the CryoEM maps by the existence of preferred orientations; the latter is achieved by a change of the optimization approach that avoids the so-called ``attraction problem'', and by the introduction of a new type of geometrical priors. It does so fully \textit{ab initio}, using deep learning training/inference steps without resorting to more traditional optimization approaches, and generating highly accurate initial reconstructions. We present maps as both homogeneous (consensus) maps and a full conformational landscape for analyzing flexibility and heterogeneity. Thanks to its Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, ReconSIREN distributes the estimation workload across independent experts, improving optimization efficiency and simplifying the process.
